phonemes.desc: Voiceless alveolar sibilant [s], as in English 'see'; Old Norse initial s is plain and unaspirated.
Short close front [i], held brief — Old Norse short i, not the long í; the name is a single light syllable.
Written f but sounded [v] — Old Norse f after a vowel was the voiced fricative, as in modern Icelandic Sif, where the name is still pronounced 'seev'.

pronunciation.approximation: 'SEEV' — one syllable, the vowel short and bright, the final f voiced to v; never 'siff' with an English double-f hiss.

kin.label: Old Norse
kin.form: Sif, wife of Þórr; beside the common noun sif (plural sifjar), 'affinity, relation by marriage' — the goddess's name is the abstract noun of kinship made personal.

kin.label: Modern Icelandic
kin.form: Sif, a living given name in Iceland, pronounced with the voiced final fricative to this day.

kin.label: English cognates
kin.form: sib, sibling, and gossip (from Old English god-sibb, 'sponsor at baptism') — the same inherited root of kinship, worn down into ordinary words.

pronunciation.note: Sif is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the normalized Old Norse form is already plain ASCII — no diacritic, no distinctive letter for the ASCII alphabet to lose. The goddess of the golden hair needs no rescued glyph; only the capital distinguishes the restored form from the input.

domains.title: Earth, Harvest
domains.subtitle: The Golden-Haired Wife of Thor
domains.lead: Sif, the golden-haired wife of [[thor|Þórr]], is one of the quietest figures in the Edda and one of the most consequential. When [[loki|Loki]] sheared off her hair in mischief, Þórr's rage forced the trickster down to the dwarfs — and the forges that answered made not only her new hair of living gold but Gungnir, Skíðblaðnir, Draupnir, Gullinbursti, and Mjölnir itself. Her name is the Old Norse word for kinship-by-marriage, sif, and the corpus keeps her exactly there: the bond at the centre of the thunder-god's house, mother of [[ullr|Ullr]], counted mother of Þrúðr, the one voice in Lokasenna that pours Loki mead and speaks him fair.

cards.name: The Golden Hair
cards.desc: The hair of wrought gold the sons of Ívaldi made for Sif, which grew to her head like living hair — Loki's shearing undone by dwarfish craft, and the seed of every treasure that followed.

cards.name: The Crystal Cup
cards.desc: The cup of ancient mead Sif herself poured for Loki in Ægir's hall, hailing him in the one courteous speech of Lokasenna — answered, as courtesy was there, with slander.

cards.name: Mjölnir from the Wager
cards.desc: The hammer of Þórr, forged by Brokkr and Sindri in the contest Loki set running when he cut Sif's hair — the greatest weapon of the Æsir, born of a theft undone.

cards.name: Ullr, Her Son
cards.desc: The archer on skis, god of the yew-bow, whom Gylfaginning names as Sif's son and Þórr's stepson — proof of a union before the thunder-god, of which the sources say nothing more.

symbols.name: The golden hair
symbols.meaning: Sif's defining attribute — shorn by Loki, remade in living gold by the sons of Ívaldi; read since Grimm as the ripe corn of the harvest field

symbols.name: The crystal cup of mead
symbols.meaning: Her single speech in Lokasenna — hospitality offered to the one guest no one else would serve

symbols.name: Mjölnir
symbols.meaning: The hammer that exists because her hair was cut — the wager's greatest prize

symbols.name: Gungnir and Skíðblaðnir
symbols.meaning: Óðinn's spear and Freyr's ship, made in the same commission that remade her hair — her restoration underwriting the gods' whole arsenal

symbols.name: Þrúðheimr
symbols.meaning: The 'world of strength' where her household stands — the fields of Thrúdheimr, Þórr's realm, her home

mythology.lead: Sif's mythology is short in line-count and enormous in consequence: one act of malice against her sets the forges of the dwarfs to work, and the gods' six greatest treasures come out of the fire. Snorri tells the hair-myth whole; the Poetic Edda gives her two smaller scenes — a cup of mead poured for Loki, and a taunt flung at Þórr across the water — and Gylfaginning names her son. Beyond that the corpus is silent, and the silence is data: the tradition kept her at the centre of Þórr's household and gave her no wars of her own.

myths.title: The Shearing of the Golden Hair
myths.text:
Loki Laufeyjarson, Snorri begins, did this for mischief: he cut off all Sif's hair. When Þórr came home and learned it, he seized Loki and would have broken every bone in him, had Loki not sworn to go to the svartálfar and have them make for Sif a head of hair from gold — hair that would grow like other hair. So Loki went to the dwarfs called the sons of Ívaldi, and they made the hair, and it grew to her head the moment it was set there, as if it were her own.

The episode is told in a handful of sentences, but its logic is exact: the injury is domestic, the redress is craft, and the restitution exceeds the loss. Sif does not speak in her own myth — the shearing, the oath, and the making all happen around her — and the tradition leaves her golden hair standing where nature left the first.

myths.title: The Wager That Forged Mjölnir
myths.text:
The sons of Ívaldi did not stop at the hair: in the same commission they made Gungnir, the spear that never misses, for [[odinn|Óðinn]], and Skíðblaðnir, the best of ships, for [[freyr|Freyr]]. Then Loki wagered his own head with the dwarf Brokkr that Brokkr's brother Sindri could not make three treasures as good. In the forge Sindri laid gold, a boar's hide, and iron in the fire in turn, while Loki, in fly-shape, stung the bellows-worker — and out came Draupnir the dripping ring, Gullinbursti the golden-bristled boar, and Mjölnir, the hammer whose handle came short only because the fly stung Brokkr's eyelid at the last draw.

The Æsir judged Mjölnir the best of all the treasures, because with it the gods have their surest defence against the rime-giants. Loki saved his head on a quibble — his neck was not in the wager — and had his lips sewn up for the pleasure of it. Count the consequence of one shorn head of hair: the spear of Óðinn, the ship of Freyr, the ring, the boar, and the hammer of [[thor|Þórr]] all exist because Sif lost her hair.

myths.title: The Crystal Cup
myths.text:
In Ægir's hall, as Loki works down the company with slander and no one escapes — not the serving-woman Fimafengr, not the gods' wives — Sif alone rises and pours him mead in a crystal cup, and speaks the flyting's one courteous stanza: 'Hail to thee, Loki, and take the crystal cup, full of ancient mead; so may you say that I alone, among the Æsir's kin, am without blame.' It is a bid for exemption, gracefully made, by the one person in the hall who tries hospitality instead of abuse.

Loki's answer is the flyting's coldest stroke: he grants she would be blameless indeed, wary and shy of men, were it not that he knows one who lay with her and drew the mighty Þórr's wife from home — 'and that was I, wretched one.' Whether the charge is truth or the poem's purest malice the text does not say; the Poetic Edda offers the accusation and no verdict, and Sif speaks no second stanza.

myths.title: The Taunt on the Shore
myths.text:
In Hárbarðsljóð, Óðinn in ferryman's disguise keeps Þórr waiting on the wrong side of the sound, and among the gibes he flings across the water is one aimed at the home Þórr cannot get back to: 'Sif has a lover at home; him you will want to meet.' The poem gives the charge no support and no sequel — it is one dart in a long volley, meant to sting a husband detained abroad, and it leans on the same rumour Lokasenna spent a stanza on.

Between the two poems the scholarly tradition has made what little can honestly be made: the eddic poets twice insinuate and never narrate, and no surviving myth shows Sif unfaithful. The taunts are evidence about the poets' taste for needling Þórr, not about the goddess.

myths.title: Ullr, Sif's Son
myths.text:
In Snorri's catalogue of the Æsir comes the genealogy that opens the one door in Sif's story: '[[ullr|Ullr]] is the name of a son of Sif and a stepson of Þórr. He is such a good archer and so fast on skis that no one can compete with him; he is also fair of face and has a warrior's skill.' Stepson — the word is the whole of it. Sif had a child before the thunder-god, by a father no source names, and the speculation that has filled the gap since (a frost-god, an older husband of the earth) is speculation, not attestation.

Snorri's kennings keep the household straight thereafter: Þórr is 'husband of Sif, stepfather of Ullr, father of [[modi|Móði]] and [[magni|Magni]] and Þrúðr' — Magni by the giantess Járnsaxa, Þrúðr counted as Sif's daughter in the reference tradition. The goddess whose name means kinship-by-marriage presides, appropriately, over the Edda's most blended household.

lore.syncretism: Sif has attracted exactly one great comparative reading, and it begins with her hair. Jacob Grimm, in the Deutsche Mythologie, took the shearing and the golden regrowth as a nature myth: Sif's hair is the ripe corn, Loki's shearing the harvest or the blight, and the dwarfs' gold the field that grows back golden — a reading that made her a Germanic harvest-goddess beside Demeter and the corn-mothers of folklore, and that matches the way the corpus ties her to Þórr, the farmer's weather-god. Twentieth-century scholarship cooled on the certainty without abandoning the observation: Simek and Turville-Petre note that the sources never call her an earth or harvest goddess, that her name means only 'kinship by marriage', and that the corn-gold reading is interpretation laid over a myth that explains itself well enough as the aetiology of the gods' treasures. The clean statement is the lexicon's own: her sphere in the tradition is the household and its bonds; the harvest is what modern readers, following Grimm, have grown in her golden hair.
lore.culturalLegacy: Sif's afterlife runs on two tracks, one scholarly and one popular. In the scholarly line she is the type-case of the Edda's reticence about goddesses: a figure with no cult record and one great myth, whose golden hair made her, from Grimm onward, the default Germanic corn-goddess of the comparative handbooks, and whose name — plain sif, 'affinity' — became the standing example of a theonym that is simply an abstract noun. In the popular line her golden hair carried her into every Victorian retelling of the gods, and modern popular culture has borrowed her outright — most visibly as the Marvel comics and film character — usually trading the wife of the sources for a swordswoman. Modern Heathen and Ásatrú communities keep the older reading, hailing her at harvest rites as the golden-haired one, patroness of grain, marriage, and household bonds. And her quietest legacy is lexical: the root of her name lives on in English, unbeknownst to its speakers, in sib, sibling, and gossip — kinship worn down into ordinary speech, which is exactly what her name always meant.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Sif is the Edda's study in how much weight a silent figure can bear. She speaks one stanza in the whole corpus — a cup of mead, a courteous wish to be counted blameless — and is answered with the flyting's crudest accusation. She is sheared, restored, taunted about, and never once given an adventure of her own; and yet the tradition built the gods' entire armoury on her injury. Gungnir, Skíðblaðnir, Draupnir, Gullinbursti, Mjölnir: take away Loki's shears and the Æsir face Ragnarǫk unarmed. The myths do not say this. They simply arrange that the greatest weapons in the North descend from a wrong done to the woman whose name means kinship.

Perhaps that is the point the name was always making. Sif is not the goddess of a thing — not thunder, not wisdom, not the sea — but of a relation: the bond that makes a household out of separate lives. The corpus honours her in its own idiom by making her household the most blended in Ásgarðr — a stepson of unknown father, sons by a giantess, a daughter of strength — and by routing every treasure of the gods through her golden head. Grimm read the hair as corn; the Edda read it as kinship. Both readings agree on the essential: what she is, grows back.
lore.originalScriptNote: The name is preserved in medieval Icelandic manuscripts in the Latin alphabet as Sif — Old Norse (North Germanic), attested in the Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda (Lokasenna, Hárbarðsljóð) and the codices of Snorri's Edda — beside the common noun sif (plural sifjar), 'affinity, relation by marriage'. The Viking-Age runic rendering in the Younger Futhark is ᛋᛁᚠ (s-i-f): ᛋ (sól) writes /s/, ᛁ (ís) writes /i/, and ᚠ (fé) writes both /f/ and the voiced fricative the manuscripts spell f — the short-twig row underspecifying nothing that matters here, though no runic attestation of the theonym itself survives. The normalized form is plain ASCII — no diacritic, no distinctive letter — which fixes the name in Tier 2. Because it is pure ASCII, its domain was registered in the ordinary way long ago: sif.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

lore.archaeology: Sif is a wholly textual goddess: no runestone invokes her, no votive deposit names her, and no image can be securely identified with her — a silence she shares with most of the ásynjur, who appear in verse and prose but rarely, if ever, in dedications. Her attestation hangs on the manuscript witnesses of the two Eddas: the Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda for Lokasenna and Hárbarðsljóð, and the Codex Regius and related codices of Snorri's Edda for the Skáldskaparmál hair-myth and the Gylfaginning genealogy that names Ullr her son. No certain place-name contains her name, though the root sif- is bound up with ordinary words for kinship across the Germanic languages; and while the Younger Futhark rendering ᛋᛁᚠ is unambiguous, no Viking-Age carving of the theonym has ever been read. The material afterlife of her myth is real but indirect: the treasures her shearing produced — Mjölnir above all — are among the most depicted objects of the Viking Age, worn as amulets in thousands of graves, so that the consequence of her one great scene is archaeologically everywhere while she herself is nowhere.
